mechanism.title: Isolation along the whole request path
steps: Identity: authenticate the user, then resolve their tenant memberships on the server. The active tenant is one the user belongs to, chosen from the token or session.

Propagation: pass the verified tenant in a signed internal token or request context to every downstream service, queue message and scheduled job. Jobs that process many tenants should loop and set the context for each one explicitly.

Data enforcement: in pooled tables, use row-level security as a backstop under application filters. In bridged or siloed designs, choose the connection from the verified tenant through one routing function, and test that it never falls back to a default.
Side channels: prefix cache keys, search indexes, object paths and queue topics with the tenant. Per-tenant encryption keys let you prove separation and crypto-shred one tenant on exit.
Capacity: give each tenant quotas and rate limits, and move bulk work to queues with per-tenant concurrency caps. Graduate very large tenants to their own shard or silo.
Verification: run cross-tenant tests for every endpoint and export, and log authorisation denials with both the caller tenant and the target tenant so attempts stand out.

useWhen: Any SaaS where customers’ data must never mix
Enterprise tiers with contractual isolation or data-residency terms
avoidWhen: Single-tenant deployments, where the tenant boundary is the deployment itself
Early prototypes with one customer, where a tenant_id column and tests are enough for now

rows: Stronger separation of data, shared compute
Many schemas to migrate; connection routing
Strongest; a bug leaks one tenant at most
Highest cost; fleet management at scale
Matches isolation to what each customer pays for
Two code paths to test and operate

numbers.title: What pooling saves, and what it risks
assumptions: Silo database at least $150 a month each (illustrative)
steps: All pool: $9,000 a month, about $1.80 per tenant, 83 times cheaper
Risk: in the pool, one missing filter can expose all 5,000 tenants, which is why row-level security and cross-tenant tests are not optional
numbers.result: A hybrid gives enterprise tenants silos for about a third more than pure pooling, while the pool stays protected by database-level policies.

india.title: PostgreSQL row security in practice
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL documentation explains that when row-level security is enabled on a table and no policy exists, a default-deny policy applies, so no rows are visible or modifiable. Superusers and roles with the BYPASSRLS attribute always bypass row security. Table owners normally bypass it too, unless the table is altered with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY. The AWS SaaS Tenant Isolation Strategies whitepaper describes the silo, bridge and pool models and treats isolation as something enforced at every layer, not only in the database.

pitfalls.trap: Taking the tenant id from a request header
pitfalls.say: I derive it from the verified token and check membership; client-supplied tenant ids are just input.

pitfalls.trap: Relying on application WHERE clauses alone in a pooled design
pitfalls.say: Add row-level security as a backstop and force it for the table owner.

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting the cache and search index
pitfalls.say: Tenant-prefix every key and index, and include them in cross-tenant tests.

takeaways: Silo, bridge and pool trade cost against blast radius
The tenant comes from verified credentials and travels with every call
Row-level security backstops application filters in pooled tables
Caches, indexes, queues and quotas need tenant isolation too

interactive.title: Whose data does the request see?
interactive.prompt: The app sets app.tenant_id once per pooled connection at request start, but only when a request has a tenant. A nightly admin report runs a query on a connection last used by tenant B.

choices.label: Tenant B’s rows, left over from the previous request
choices.feedback: Right: session state outlives the request on a pooled connection.

choices.label: No rows, because no tenant is set
choices.feedback: A tenant is set: tenant B’s, from the last borrower.

choices.label: An error, because the policy needs a tenant
choices.feedback: The setting exists, so the policy runs with the stale value.

interactive.reveal: Scope the setting to the transaction, reset it on release, and make an empty setting match nothing.

seeAlso.why: Object-level access checks, the per-request half of tenant isolation
Connection pooling, where session state can leak between tenants
Per-tenant rate limits and quotas against noisy neighbours

title: Surviving DDoS: Absorb, Filter and Shed
objectives: Tell volumetric, protocol and application-layer floods apart
Explain why floods must be absorbed at the edge, before the origin
Defend expensive endpoints against request floods without runaway cost

cards.title: Three kinds of flood
cards.body: Volumetric attacks fill the network pipe and are measured in gigabits per second. Protocol attacks, such as SYN floods, exhaust connection tables and firewall state, and are measured in packets per second. Application-layer attacks send valid-looking HTTP requests to expensive endpoints such as search, login or checkout, and are measured in requests per second. A rule that stops one kind does nothing against the others, so identify the layer before choosing a response.

cards.title: Absorb at the edge, not at the origin
cards.body: If your data centre has a 10 Gbps uplink, a 100 Gbps flood fills the link upstream of your firewall, so nothing you run can drop it in time. Large anycast networks (CDNs and cloud DDoS services) advertise the same addresses from many locations, so the flood spreads across all of them and is filtered close to its sources. Your origin then accepts traffic only from the edge provider, ideally over a private connection.

cards.title: Worked example: why reflection multiplies traffic
cards.body: Reflection abuses open UDP services that send large replies to small queries. This is how to reason about it as a defender.
steps: UDP has no handshake, so a query can carry a forged source address: the victim’s
Each open service replies to that address with a much larger response
Illustrative: 60-byte queries drawing 3,000-byte replies multiply traffic 50 times, so 2 Gbps sent becomes 100 Gbps received
Defence for everyone: networks drop packets with forged source addresses (BCP 38), and operators close or rate-limit open UDP services
Defence for the victim: absorb at an anycast edge and drop unexpected UDP before it reaches the origin

cards.title: Misconception: autoscaling defeats a DDoS
cards.body: Adding servers does nothing when the link is full, because the traffic never reaches them. Against an application-layer flood, scaling turns the attack into a bill while the shared database still saturates. Put hard maximums on scaling, and filter before you scale: per-client rate limits, bot challenges on risky paths, caching that ignores junk query parameters, and load shedding that keeps checkout alive while dropping low-priority work.

cards.title: Trap: leaving the origin reachable directly
cards.body: An edge network only helps if attackers must go through it. Origin addresses leak through old DNS records, mail servers on the same host, test subdomains and error pages. Once found, the origin can be flooded directly. Firewall the origin to accept only the edge provider’s address ranges or an authenticated tunnel. If the address has leaked, move to a new one.

questions.prompt: Inbound traffic is only 200 Mbps, but login receives 80,000 valid-looking requests a second from many addresses, and the database is pegged. What kind of attack is it?

choices.label: A volumetric flood that fills the link
An application-layer request flood
A reflection attack using open UDP services
A SYN flood filling the connection table

questions.explanation: Low bandwidth with many complete, valid HTTP requests that exhaust a backend is the application-layer pattern. A volumetric or reflection attack would show high bandwidth, and a SYN flood would leave half-open connections rather than completed logins.

questions.prompt: Your origin has a 10 Gbps uplink, and a 300 Gbps flood arrives. Where can it be absorbed?

choices.label: On the origin, by adding application servers
At the origin firewall, by dropping bad packets
Across a large anycast edge, before it reaches you
By raising the origin’s TCP backlog setting

questions.explanation: The link saturates upstream of everything at the origin, so only capacity larger than the attack, spread across many locations, can absorb it. Servers, firewall rules and backlog settings all sit behind the full pipe.

questions.prompt: An attacker sends 2 Gbps of 60-byte queries to open UDP services, each of which replies with 3,000 bytes to the forged source. Roughly how much traffic reaches the victim?
questions.explanation: Design implication: that is ten times a 10 Gbps uplink, so only an edge network with more capacity than the flood can absorb it.

questions.prompt: During a request flood on /search, autoscaling has grown the fleet from 20 to 400 servers. What is the main risk of letting it continue?

choices.label: The bill climbs while the database behind it still saturates
Autoscaling makes the attack traffic itself larger
New servers cannot join the load balancer mid-attack
Scaling turns off the edge cache for the site

questions.explanation: Stateless servers scale but the shared database does not, so cost rises with no gain in availability. The attack rate is set by the attacker, servers can still register, and scaling does not change cache settings.

questions.prompt: Order the response when a flood begins.

items.label: Apply the matching filter at the edge
Detect: traffic or errors far above the baseline
Review and tune the rules after the attack
Classify the layer: bandwidth, packets or requests
Shed low-priority work at the origin if it is still overloaded

questions.explanation: The layer decides the filter, so classify before acting. Shedding protects what is left, and a review makes the next attack cheaper to stop.

questions.prompt: The 2023 HTTP/2 Rapid Reset attacks opened streams and cancelled them at once, many times per connection. Why did this hurt servers so much?

choices.label: The resets used up the victims’ network bandwidth
Servers started work on each stream before it was cancelled
The resets broke the encryption on each connection
Each reset forced a new TLS handshake

questions.explanation: Cancelling a stream let the client open another at once without hitting the concurrent-stream limit, while the server had already begun work. Bandwidth was modest, TLS stayed intact, and the same connection was reused. That is why fixes limit how fast a client may reset streams.

flashcards.back: Volumetric (Gbps), protocol (packets/s and state), application (requests/s).
A flood larger than your uplink fills it before any origin defence runs.
Accept traffic only from the edge provider; move the address if it leaks.

sources.title: Google Cloud: mitigating a 398 million rps DDoS attack
AWS: How DDoS attacks work and how to protect against them
OWASP Denial of Service Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: Defence in layers, from the internet inward
steps: Edge capacity: put public endpoints behind an anycast network whose capacity is far larger than plausible attacks. It absorbs volumetric and reflection floods across many locations and drops obviously invalid packets.
Protocol protection: SYN cookies and stateless filtering at the edge keep connection tables from filling. Only well-formed, completed connections are passed on.

Request filtering: a web application firewall and per-client rate limits act on paths, headers and behaviour. Challenges are reserved for risky traffic, and rules can be switched on in minutes during an attack.
Caching: serve as much as possible from the edge, and normalise cache keys so random query strings cannot force misses.
Origin protection: accept traffic only from the edge, cap autoscaling, and shed load by priority. Keep checkout and login alive, and drop recommendations and analytics first.
Preparation: baseline normal traffic, rehearse the runbook, know how to reach your provider’s response team, and set budget alerts so an attack cannot quietly run up the bill.

useWhen: Any public-facing service that would lose money or trust when unavailable
Services with expensive endpoints such as search, login or report generation
avoidWhen: Internal-only services with no public addresses, where network controls suffice
Using challenges on every request, which harms real users and accessibility

rows: Must be in the path; a leaked origin bypasses it
Little help against valid HTTP floods
Rules need tuning; distributed bots spread load
Only cacheable content; shedding drops some real users

numbers.title: When caching saves you, and when it does not
assumptions: Attack: 1,000,000 requests a second on a product page
Edge cache hit ratio for that page: 99%
steps: With caching: 1,000,000 × 0.01 = 10,000 requests a second reach the origin, half its capacity
Attacker adds a random query string to every request; if the cache key includes it, the hit ratio drops to about 0%
Then 1,000,000 a second reach the origin, 50 times its capacity
Fix: drop unknown query parameters from the cache key and rate-limit per client, which brings origin load back under 20,000
numbers.result: Caching absorbs a request flood only when attackers cannot bust the cache, so normalise cache keys and keep per-client limits on uncached paths.

india.title: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, 2023
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: In October 2023 Google Cloud reported mitigating a DDoS attack that peaked above 398 million requests per second. That was about 7.5 times its previous record of 46 million. The attack used a new HTTP/2 technique called Rapid Reset, which opens and cancels streams in quick succession, and was tracked as CVE-2023-44487. Google said the two-minute attack generated more requests than Wikipedia’s reported article views for all of September 2023. Absorbing it relied on global edge capacity and load balancing, plus server fixes that limit how quickly a client can reset streams.

pitfalls.trap: Counting on autoscaling to ride out an attack
pitfalls.say: Scaling cannot clear a full link, and it bills you for request floods; I would filter at the edge and cap scaling.

pitfalls.trap: Putting a CDN in front but leaving the origin open
pitfalls.say: Firewall the origin to the edge provider’s ranges, or attackers simply go around it.

pitfalls.trap: One rule for every flood
pitfalls.say: Classify the layer first: bandwidth, packets and requests each need a different filter.

takeaways: Identify the layer: bandwidth, packets or requests
Absorb floods at an anycast edge larger than the attack
Hide and lock down the origin behind the edge
Filter, cache and shed before you scale

interactive.title: Will autoscaling save you?
interactive.prompt: Your origin has a 10 Gbps uplink and autoscaling up to 500 servers. A 150 Gbps UDP flood arrives at its address.

choices.label: No: the link is full before traffic reaches a server
choices.feedback: Right: the bottleneck is upstream of everything you can scale.

choices.label: Yes: more servers can absorb more traffic
choices.feedback: Servers sit behind the saturated 10 Gbps link.

choices.label: Yes, if the servers drop the UDP packets
choices.feedback: By the time packets reach a server, the link has already dropped real traffic.

interactive.reveal: Volumetric floods are absorbed by capacity larger than the attack, which in practice means an anycast edge.

seeAlso.why: Rate limiting, the core tool against application-layer floods
SSRF, another way attackers turn your own servers into their tool
Locking the origin down to edge-only traffic with network rules

title: Vulnerability Triage and Patch Management
objectives: Separate severity scores from real-world risk
Use exploitation evidence, exposure and reachability to set order
Set patch deadlines a team can actually meet

cards.title: Severity is not the same as risk
cards.body: A CVSS base score (0 to 10) describes how bad a vulnerability would be in a typical setup: how it is reached, what privileges it needs and what it affects. It does not say whether anyone is exploiting it, whether your service is exposed, or whether your code even calls the flawed function. Risk is likelihood times impact in your context, and the score is only one input to it.

cards.title: Signals of likelihood: known exploitation and EPSS
cards.body: Two public signals help with likelihood. CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue lists flaws with evidence of exploitation in the wild. FIRST’s Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) estimates the probability that a flaw will see exploitation activity in the next 30 days. Combine them with exposure: an internet-facing gateway with a known-exploited flaw outranks a higher-scored flaw in an internal batch tool.

cards.title: Worked example: triaging 1,200 scanner findings
cards.body: A container scan across 60 images reports 1,200 findings. The team can fix about 25 a week.
steps: Deduplicate: the same library flaw in 40 images is one fix, which cuts the list to about 300 distinct items
Pull to the top anything that is known-exploited or has a high exploitation probability
Check exposure and reachability: is the component internet-facing, and does untrusted input reach the vulnerable code?
Set a deadline by tier, such as days for exposed and exploited, weeks for exposed, the normal cycle for the rest
Record each accepted risk with an owner, a reason and an expiry date

cards.title: Misconception: “critical” means drop everything
cards.body: Take a 9.8 in a test library that never ships, and a 7.5 that is being exploited in your VPN appliance. The second is the emergency. Treating every high score as urgent burns the team out and buries the few findings that matter. Rank by exploitation evidence, exposure and reachability, and use the score to break ties.

cards.title: Trap: wanting to patch fast without being able to
cards.body: Most delay is not in deciding but in shipping. Typical causes are an unknown inventory, no automated tests to trust an upgrade, and manual deploys. Keep a software bill of materials, so you know where a component runs within minutes of an advisory. Take routine dependency updates in small, tested steps every week, so an urgent bump is ordinary work rather than a leap across two years of versions.

questions.prompt: What does a CVSS base score of 9.8 tell you on its own?

choices.label: The flaw is being exploited in the wild right now
Your service calls the vulnerable code
The flaw would be severe if exploited in a typical setup
The vendor’s patch is safe to deploy untested

questions.explanation: The base score describes intrinsic severity. Exploitation evidence comes from sources such as the KEV catalogue, reachability from your own analysis, and patch safety from your tests.

questions.prompt: Finding one: CVSS 9.1 in a library no exposed service loads. Finding two: CVSS 7.2, on the known-exploited list, in your internet-facing gateway. Which first?

choices.label: The 9.1, because the higher base score sets the order
The 7.2 gateway flaw, which is exploited and exposed
Both together in one release next quarter
Neither until a second scanner confirms them

questions.explanation: Active exploitation plus internet exposure makes the gateway flaw the likely breach. The base score alone ignores both. Waiting a quarter or for a second scanner leaves an exploited, exposed hole open.

questions.prompt: A scanner flags a parsing flaw in a library your build includes. What reduces its urgency most?

choices.label: The library is popular and actively maintained
The service runs inside a container
Evidence that no untrusted input reaches that parser
The finding has been open a while without incident

questions.explanation: If attacker-controlled data cannot reach the flawed code, it cannot be exploited through that path. You still patch, but on the normal cycle. Popularity, containers and quiet history do not stop an exploit that can reach the code.

questions.prompt: You have 300 open findings and fix 25 a week, while 15 new ones arrive each week. How many weeks until the backlog is clear?
questions.formula: backlog / (fixed per week − new per week)
questions.workedAnswer: Net progress is 25 − 15 = 10 a week, so 300 / 10 = 30 weeks.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: ignoring new arrivals gives 12 weeks, a plan that will slip badly. To clear it in 10 weeks you need 300 / 10 + 15 = 45 fixes a week.

questions.prompt: Order a triage pass over a new scanner report.

items.label: Set a fix deadline by tier
Group duplicate findings into single fixes
Check exposure and reachability for each item
Track accepted risks with an owner and expiry
Raise exploited and likely-exploited items to the top

questions.explanation: Shrink the list, rank by likelihood, refine with your own context, then commit to dates and record the exceptions.

questions.prompt: A critical, actively exploited flaw hits the web server software on 400 internet-facing hosts. The vendor fix is out, and your normal release window is monthly.

approaches.label: Mitigate within hours, then roll out the fix within days
Wait for the monthly window to keep change control simple
Put the hosts behind a VPN for good and skip the patch

rationaleOptions.label: Known exploitation makes delay the larger risk
A mitigation buys time while the patch is tested
Change windows matter more than exposure
A network move removes the need to patch

rationaleConflicts.r3: An exploited, exposed flaw is exactly the case emergency change exists for.
rationaleConflicts.r4: The flaw is still there for anyone who reaches the VPN, and public sites cannot hide anyway.

questions.explanation: Exploited and exposed means emergency: mitigate now (a WAF rule or disabling the feature), patch fast, verify.

flashcards.back: CVSS rates severity in general; risk adds exploitation, exposure and reachability in your system.
KEV: evidence of exploitation in the wild. EPSS: probability of exploitation activity in 30 days.
Weeks to clear = backlog / (fix rate − arrival rate).

sources.title: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4: Enterprise Patch Management Planning
OWASP Vulnerable Dependency Management Cheat Sheet
OWASP Top 10:2025, Software Supply Chain Failures

mechanism.title: A triage pipeline that keeps up
steps: Inventory: generate a software bill of materials for every build and image, and keep a list of what is deployed where. Without it, every advisory starts with a hunt.
Collect: scanners for dependencies, images and hosts feed one queue. Deduplicate by component and version, so one upgrade closes many findings.
Enrich: add the CVSS score, known-exploited status, EPSS probability, and your own context, such as internet exposure, data sensitivity and whether the vulnerable function is reachable.
Decide: map each finding to a tier with a deadline, and choose a response. Patch or upgrade; mitigate (configuration change, WAF rule, disabling a feature); or accept with an owner and an expiry.
Ship: small, frequent dependency updates through automated tests and staged rollout, so urgent fixes use the same path as routine ones.
Measure: track time to remediate by tier and the backlog trend. If arrivals outpace fixes, the plan is fiction, so add capacity or reduce the attack surface.

useWhen: Any team running third-party code, which is every team
Regulated environments that must show patch timelines
avoidWhen: Treating every scanner finding as an emergency, which drowns the real ones
Waivers with no expiry, which quietly become permanent

rows: Whether it is exploited or reachable in your system
New flaws before evidence is collected
Whether attackers can reach the code
Future code changes that make it reachable

numbers.title: Will this backlog ever clear?
steps: Net burn-down: 25 − 15 = 10 a week
Time to clear: 300 / 10 = 30 weeks
To clear in 10 weeks: 300 / 10 + 15 = 45 fixes a week, nearly double the current rate
Alternative: cut arrivals by dropping unused dependencies; at 5 new a week, 300 / 20 = 15 weeks
numbers.result: Backlog plans must include the arrival rate. Removing unused dependencies is often cheaper than hiring more fixers.

india.title: NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 4 on patching as maintenance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-40 Revision 4 (April 2022) defines enterprise patch management as identifying, prioritising, acquiring, installing and verifying the installation of patches, updates and upgrades. It frames patching as preventive maintenance and a normal cost of doing business, not an exceptional event. It recommends an enterprise strategy that simplifies and operationalises patching, and maintenance plans for groups of assets with similar risk, so that routine updates and emergency fixes follow known paths. The OWASP Top 10:2025 widened its former vulnerable-components category into Software Supply Chain Failures (A03).

pitfalls.trap: Sorting the backlog by CVSS score alone
pitfalls.say: Rank by exploitation evidence and exposure first, then use the score to break ties between findings that are otherwise equally urgent.

pitfalls.trap: Promising a 7-day patch SLA with monthly manual deploys
pitfalls.say: The deadline must match the delivery pipeline, so automate updates and rollouts first.

pitfalls.trap: Accepting risks with no end date
pitfalls.say: Every exception gets an owner and an expiry, and is reviewed when it lapses.

takeaways: CVSS measures severity; risk needs likelihood and context
Known exploitation and exposure decide what is urgent
Deduplicate and check reachability before scheduling work
Plan with arrival rates, and make patching routine

interactive.title: Which goes first?
interactive.prompt: Three findings arrive on Monday. You can fix one today.

choices.label: CVSS 9.8 in a test-only tool that never ships
choices.feedback: Severe in theory, but not present in production.

choices.label: CVSS 6.5, known-exploited, in the internet-facing login proxy
choices.feedback: Right: exploited and exposed beats a higher score.

choices.label: CVSS 8.1 in an internal admin tool behind single sign-on
choices.feedback: Real but less exposed; it goes on the short-deadline tier.

interactive.reveal: Exploitation evidence and exposure set urgency; the base score refines it.

seeAlso.why: Supply-chain security, where these dependencies come from
Threat modelling supplies the exposure context for triage
Audit logs help confirm whether a flaw was exploited before the patch

title: Protecting Personal Data: Minimise, Pseudonymise, Delete
objectives: Apply data minimisation to forms, logs and analytics
Distinguish pseudonymised data from anonymous data
Design deletion that reaches backups, indexes and processors

cards.title: Data you never collected cannot leak
cards.body: Minimisation means collecting, using and keeping only what a stated purpose needs. An age gate needs “over 18: yes”, not a date of birth. Delivery needs an address until the parcel arrives, not forever. Apply the same test to logs, analytics events, support exports and test databases, where copies multiply quietly. Every field you drop is one you never have to secure, disclose or delete.

cards.title: Pseudonymised is not anonymous
cards.body: Replacing names with random ids or keyed hashes is pseudonymisation. Anyone with the key, the mapping table or enough other attributes can still re-identify people, so the data remains personal data. Combinations of quasi-identifiers such as postcode, birth date and sex single out a large share of people. Anonymisation needs more: aggregate, generalise (age bands, regions), suppress small groups, or add noise. Then test that individuals cannot reasonably be singled out.

cards.title: Worked example: tokenising phone numbers for analytics
cards.body: Analysts need to count repeat callers without seeing phone numbers.
steps: At ingest, a tokenisation service swaps each phone number for a random token and keeps the mapping in a locked-down vault
Analytics tables hold only tokens, so joins and repeat counts still work
Support staff who need a real number call the vault, which checks their role and logs the lookup
Deleting a customer deletes their mapping; their tokens no longer lead to a person, though rows still link to each other
Reports publish only aggregates for groups of at least 10 people

cards.title: Misconception: hashing an email address anonymises it
cards.body: An unkeyed hash such as SHA-256 of an email address is easy to reverse. Hash a list of known addresses and match the results. It is also a stable identifier that links datasets across companies. If you need a pseudonym, use an HMAC with a secret key held in a KMS, and still treat the output as personal data. If you need no link back at all, aggregate instead.

cards.title: Trap: deleting from the main database only
cards.body: A person’s data also sits in backups, logs, search indexes, caches, the analytics warehouse, email tools and third-party processors. Keep a data map of where each category flows. Run deletion as a pipeline that reaches each store and each processor. Let backups age out on a known schedule, or encrypt per person and destroy the key. Record that the request was completed, without recording the deleted data itself.

questions.prompt: A sign-up form must confirm users are adults. What should it store?

choices.label: The full date of birth, in case the rules change
A yes or no result of the check, and when it ran
A scan of the user’s identity document
The date of birth, encrypted in the same database

questions.explanation: The purpose needs only the outcome. A date of birth is a strong identifier, and encrypting it in the same database still keeps it. An identity scan is far more sensitive than the question needs. “In case the rules change” is exactly the reasoning minimisation rejects.

questions.prompt: An analytics table swaps names for random ids but keeps full postcode, birth date and sex. Is it anonymous?

choices.label: Yes, because no names or emails remain
Yes, if the random ids are 128 bits long
No: those three fields together single out many people
No, unless the table is encrypted at rest

questions.explanation: Quasi-identifiers combine to re-identify individuals, whatever the id length. Removing direct identifiers is not enough. Encryption at rest protects stolen disks, not people who can query the table, so it does not make data anonymous.

questions.prompt: Why is SHA-256 of an email address a weak pseudonym?

choices.label: Anyone can hash a list of known emails and match them
SHA-256 outputs collide too often for email addresses
The hash is longer than most email addresses
Hashes cannot be used as join keys

questions.explanation: Email addresses are guessable and widely leaked, so an unkeyed hash is reversed by lookup. SHA-256 collisions are not a practical concern, length is irrelevant, and stable hashes make excellent join keys, which is part of the danger.

questions.prompt: Nightly backups are kept for 35 days and weekly backups for 12 weeks. A customer is deleted from the live database today. After how many days is their data gone from all backups, if nothing is restored?
questions.formula: the longest retention period, in days
questions.workedAnswer: The longest-lived copy is a weekly backup: 12 × 7 = 84 days.
questions.explanation: Design implication: tell the customer about the backup window in your privacy notice, or crypto-shred per-customer keys to make the copies unreadable at once.

questions.prompt: Order a deletion request so that no copy is missed.

items.label: Delete or anonymise in live stores, and tell processors to do the same
Verify that the requester owns the account
Record that the request was completed
Use the data map to find every store holding their data
Let backups expire on schedule, or destroy the customer’s key

questions.explanation: Verify first, so deletion cannot be abused. Map, delete, handle backups, then keep evidence of completion without the data itself.

questions.prompt: A vault maps card numbers to random tokens for the rest of the system. Where does the remaining risk concentrate?

choices.label: In the analytics tables that store tokens
In the vault and the services allowed to detokenise
In the token format, which can be reversed with maths
In the link between the browser and the CDN

questions.explanation: Random tokens carry no information, so they reveal nothing without the vault. Risk concentrates where real values can be recovered, which is why the vault gets strict access control and logging. That is also why tokenisation can shrink the scope of a compliance audit.

flashcards.back: Does this purpose need this field, at this precision, for this long?
Pseudonymised data can be re-identified with a key or other attributes; it is still personal data.
Live stores, logs, indexes, caches, warehouse, processors and backups.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-122: Protecting the Confidentiality of PII
NIST SP 800-188: De-Identifying Government Data Sets
OWASP User Privacy Protection Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: Privacy engineering, step by step
steps: Inventory and classify: list each personal-data field, its purpose, its sensitivity (contact, financial, health, location) and every store and processor it flows to. This data map drives everything else.
Minimise at the source: drop fields without a purpose, reduce precision (age band, city), and stop personal data entering logs and analytics events in the first place.
Separate identities from activity: tokenise or pseudonymise direct identifiers with keyed functions, and keep the mapping in a vault with its own access policy and audit log.
Control access: give people and services the least access their role needs, mask fields in support tools, and log every detokenisation or bulk export.
Set retention per category: delete or aggregate data when its purpose ends, automatically, with backups on a known expiry. Per-person keys enable crypto-shredding where backups cannot be edited.
Handle requests and breaches: a tested pipeline for access and deletion requests, and an incident plan that knows which data categories each system holds.

useWhen: Any system holding data about identifiable people
Analytics and machine-learning pipelines that copy production data
avoidWhen: Claiming aggregated or public data needs no thought, since joins can re-identify people
Building custom anonymisation for high-risk releases without expert review

rows: Less data to protect or lose
Product pressure to collect “just in case”
Still personal data; key and mapping must be guarded
Small groups and repeated queries can leak
Key management and per-person key overhead

numbers.title: How long does deletion really take?
assumptions: Warehouse rebuilt from live data weekly
steps: Live database and search index: deleted today by the pipeline
Warehouse: gone at the next weekly rebuild, within 7 days
Logs: aged out within 30 days, if personal data was logged at all
Backups: the longest copy is weekly, 12 × 7 = 84 days
numbers.result: Deletion completes in 84 days unless per-person keys are destroyed, so state that window honestly or shorten backup retention.

india.title: NIST guidance on personal data
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-122 recommends that organisations minimise the use, collection and retention of personally identifiable information to what is strictly necessary for their purpose. It also recommends assigning an impact level to each set of PII, so that safeguards match the harm a breach would cause. NIST SP 800-188 describes de-identification techniques and warns that removing direct identifiers alone may not prevent re-identification. India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 likewise expects personal data to be erased once its purpose is served or consent is withdrawn, which makes a working deletion pipeline a legal need, not a nicety.

pitfalls.trap: Calling hashed emails anonymous
pitfalls.say: An unkeyed hash is reversible by lookup; at best it is a pseudonym and still personal data.

pitfalls.trap: Deleting from the main database and calling it done
pitfalls.say: Use the data map to reach logs, indexes, warehouses, processors and backups.

pitfalls.trap: Collecting fields in case they are useful later
pitfalls.say: Each field needs a purpose and a retention period, or we do not collect it.

takeaways: Collect only what a purpose needs, at the precision it needs
Pseudonymised data is still personal; anonymisation needs aggregation and testing

interactive.title: What does the leaked export expose?
interactive.prompt: A support export with columns user_id, SHA-256(email), city and last order is posted publicly by mistake.

choices.label: The emails of anyone on a list the finder already has
choices.feedback: Right: hash the candidate list and match.

choices.label: Nothing personal, since the emails are hashed
choices.feedback: Unkeyed hashes of guessable values are reversible by lookup.

choices.label: Only the cities and orders
choices.feedback: The hashes link straight back to known addresses.

interactive.reveal: Minimise exports, and use keyed pseudonyms or aggregates when analysts need joins.
